pr_title: http,http2: add abort signal to server requests
pr_body:
Add support for getting a signal from http/http2 server requests which is aborted when the requests themselves are aborted.

fixes: https://github.com/nodejs/node/issues/37661

I think that this feature makes sense, and is similar to what [Fetch](https://fetch.spec.whatwg.org/#request-signal) has.  I haven't added tests or changed docs yet, as I'd like to see if there's support for this feature. If other people think this is a good idea - I'll happily contribute tests and docs for this as well.

review_comments: should we provide some access to the `AbortController`?

If we're only looking at the use case presented here, I don't think so, but there's a larger consideration here that makes me question this PR. The approach here uses the abort on the request as the trigger, but that's not always reliable and ignores the other reasons why a request flow may be aborted. There are other scenarios where a request flow would be aborted where aborting the actual streams may not be desirable. In those cases, it would be better for the AbortController to exist independent of the Request object, and for the Request to optionally register itself as an `abort` event listener (rather than the other way around seen in this PR).

tl;dr ... I'm not sure if this PR is the right approach.

IMO, putting aside the correctness of my code, I was wondering if the signal should be limited to just aborted requests - maybe the signal should notify on completion? I can see how that would be useful as well (although semantically it might be confusing)

I think that if the AbortCobtroller will be exposed then it should be a method and not a getter.

That said I think not exposing it makes sense too.

I also am not sure regarding whether it should signal completion or specifically "aborted"

Well, if the `signal` is just limited to aborted requests, the request object *already* exposes an `aborted` event that user land can tap in to (just like this PR does). The `AbortSignal` just becomes redundant.

> The AbortSignal just becomes redundant

I think the feature request was since other APIs take AbortSignals this would let you pass the signal to those APIs directly instead of creating an AbortController, listening to `"aborted"` etc. If everything takes an AbortSignal you can just pass signals and not worry about events all the way which makes it easier to write safer and "obviously correct" code.

That said I have no idea if it should listen to completion or just "aborted" 😅

Other platforms also have similar features. For example [.NET](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/mvc/models/model-binding?view=aspnetcore-3.1#cancellationtoken) can either [DI a CancellationToken](https://andrewlock.net/using-cancellationtokens-in-asp-net-core-mvc-controllers/#using-cancellationtokens-in-your-mvc-actions) or be used directly from [HttpContext.RequestAborted](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.aspnetcore.http.httpcontext.requestaborted?view=aspnetcore-5.0) (Cancellation Tokens are pretty similar to AbortSignal).

I agree with @benjamingr that it gives you a simple way to use signals "all the way down".
It could be beneficial for this to be moved to a utility function that is called by the two `get signal()` to avoid the code duplication.

The abort here should maybe be fired in a `process.nextTick()`, otherwise there won't be any opportunity for any listeners to attach before the `abort()` is called. That could be fine, but it's not clear. What do you think @mcollina
I agree
I think that's probably a good idea @jasnell and the tradeoff I did when adding this API elsewhere.

I understand the reason for this change, but if I understand correctly this would mean that whoever is using the signal is using it incorrectly, as they should always check if it's `aborted` anyway, before adding a listener.
I think accessing a property should not have any side effect.

I think the side effect is not observable outside of the property though so should be fine? Something about if a tree falls in a forest and no one hears.

Would you prefer an implementation where every HTTP request is larger and slower because of the `AbortSignal`?

I'm fine with the lazy creation of the internal state. Calling the `abort()` inside the getter may be very surprising for folks but there's not another way of creating an `AbortController` that is already tripped so I'm not sure there's a good approach for that.

I dislike calling `abort` as well, but given the other change request the signal will always return non-aborted for the first time (as it'll move into a `process.nextTick`), so we don't have to create a tripped signal.

Honestly I don't really understand what the issue with the getter behaviour is.

It's true that we're mutating (creating and maybe aborting an AbortController in a getter), but the AbortController isn't exposed anywhere and from the API consumer point of view that fact is abstracted.

The user only gets access to a signal - so I think it's fine?
As I said, my only concern is on calling the `abort()` and that's only because I have a general dislike for getters that have potentially unexpected side effects. In this case, I think it's fine.

> Would you prefer an implementation where every HTTP request is larger and slower because of the AbortSignal?

That's the exact thing I want to prevent from happening.

Calling this `.signal()` instead of `.signal` is a clear indication that calling this method has side effects.
I agree but from the user's point of view it has 0 side effects they are all internal :)
